Fleshly
flĕsh´lĭ
adj. (pertaining to the flesh; carnal, as opposed to spiritual — Greek sarkikos)
From flesh, Old English flæsc. The Greek sarkikos means belonging to the flesh — not the body as created, but the fallen nature considered as a principle of action.

Biblical Definition

Fleshly describes what proceeds from the fallen nature rather than from the Spirit, and Scripture applies it to three things a man might not suspect. To desires: “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul” (1Pe 2:11) — and note that the war is against the soul, not merely against the body. To wisdom: “our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world” (2Co 1:12) — there is a cleverness in ministry that is of the flesh, and Paul renounces it. And, most surprisingly, to religion: “Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” (Col 2:18). The man described there is ascetic, humble in appearance, absorbed in things unseen — and Paul calls his mind fleshly. That is the sting of the word. The flesh is not merely appetite; it is self operating in any mode, including the devout one, and Paul says such observances have no value against the indulgence of the flesh. The conflict is permanent this side of glory: “the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Gal 5:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fleshly as pertaining to the flesh; carnal; not spiritual; animal; as fleshly lusts.

expand to see more

FLESH'LY, a. Pertaining to the flesh; corporeal.

2. Carnal; worldly; lascivious; as fleshly lusts.

3. Human; not celestial; not spiritual or divine.

CAR'NAL, a. Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; opposed to spiritual or regenerate.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;"

2 Corinthians 1:12 — "For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward."

Colossians 2:18 — "Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind,"

Galatians 5:17 — "For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would."

Modern Corruption

The flesh is identified with the body, so that the sins of the mind and of religion itself escape the category entirely, and asceticism is mistaken for mortification.

expand to see more

The commonest mistake with this word is to equate flesh with body and therefore to locate all fleshly sin below the neck. Colossians 2:18 destroys that reading in a phrase: vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind. The man in view is not a glutton; he is an ascetic with visions, practising voluntary humility and worshipping angels, and Paul calls his mind fleshly and says his observances are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. Pride, faction, self-display in devotion, and religious cleverness are all works of the flesh, and Galatians 5 lists hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions and heresies beside drunkenness in one catalogue.

The ancient error was to conclude that the body itself is the problem, and it has never fully left the church. Scripture teaches otherwise: God made the body, the Son took one, the Spirit indwells it as a temple, and it will be raised. What is condemned is not matter but the fallen nature that uses body and mind alike for its own ends. Hence Peter's warning that fleshly lusts war against the soul. The damage is not chiefly bodily and the remedy is not chiefly bodily either: it is walking in the Spirit, which is the one thing Galatians promises will keep a man from fulfilling the lust of the flesh.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sarkikos (G4559), fleshly, carnal — 1 Peter 2:11, 2 Corinthians 1:12, Romans 15:27; sarx (G4561), flesh; psuchikos (G5591), natural or soulish.

expand to see more

Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; 1 Peter 2:11, 2 Corinthians 1:12, 2 Corinthians 10:4 of weapons not carnal.

Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; used of the body, of human nature, and of the fallen principle of action.

Greek psuchikos (G5591) — natural, soulish; 1 Corinthians 2:14 of the natural man who receiveth not the things of the Spirit.

Colossians 2:23 states the verdict on fleshly religion: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.

Galatians 5:19-21 lists the works of the flesh, and most of the items are not bodily appetites.

Usage

"“Fleshly lusts, which war against the soul” — the war is not merely bodily."

"“Not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God” — cleverness renounced."

"“Vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind” — said of an ascetic."
